Can you tell us why -- under what circumstances would you submit an interim intelligence report?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were daily and interim intelligence reports, as you say. Their numbers are what they are. The Defence had not alerted me to the fact, I wouldn't have paid any attention to it myself, but the numbers speak for themselves. They give you the sequence of the documents that passed through the operative sector. Interim reports are also reports, regardless. They don't have a separate nomenclature, they have the same nomenclature. They are treated the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: But that wasn't my question to you. My question to you was under what circumstances you would submit an interim intelligence report. That was my question.

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever something out of the ordinary happened, something that was not expected, something that maybe it didn't get that much attention during the day, this couldn't wait for the daily report to be drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if the witness could be shown Exhibit 554. And if we could go to page 3 of the English, and there's only one page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, I'm going to direct you again to the second bullet point under the second-to-last paragraph of the B/C/S. And, Your Honours, that's the second bullet point under the last page in the English. If we could get the B/C/S back, please. Sir, again I'm referring you to the second bullet point under the second-to-last paragraph, which begins: "Meet with superior officer of the El Mudjahedin Detachment ..." During the course of your cross-examination yesterday, the question was put to you: "Do you agree that your superior --" Can we scroll down on the English, please. Thank you. Yesterday, during the course of your cross-examination, the question was put to you: "Do you agree that your superior, in a technical sense, Mr. Husic, did not know what was going on on the ground unless you informed him in writing? Would that be a fair assessment?" And the answer that you had given was: "Yes, it would." Now, in relation to the second bullet point, there's reference there to the prisoners of the Prnjavor Light Brigade being located at the El Mujahedin Detachment camp. If the 3rd Corps Intelligence Department was dependent on you for information, could you explain to us how the presence of these POWs at the El Mudjahedin Detachment camp could have reached that department?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably through the Security Service of the 35th Division on the Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, sir. Now, yesterday you had referred to a person -- you had stated that, "The only person I saw was the Emir." Can you elaborate on that answer? And let me just be a little clearer. The question that had been put to you was: "Did you have any officers that you could contact whom you could instruct and from whom you could get feedback there?" And the answer that you had given is: "I didn't know anyone --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please have a reference for this particular portion of the evidence that's being quoted, where apparently the witness said, "The only person I saw was the Emir," because I don't remember that reference, myself. If we could have the page number, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's page number 3784. The question begins at line 21, and then it continues on -- actually, it ends, it ends at 3784, so the answer ends at line 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that yesterday's evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, let me read the question out to you that was put to you. The question was: "Did you have any officers that you could contact, whom you could instruct and from whom you could get feedback there?" And you answered: "I didn't know anyone, intelligence officers or anybody else from the El Mudjahedin Detachment camp. I literally didn't know anyone. The only person I saw was the Emir. That was that one time, but that was all." Can you tell us what this person's name is, the person you referred to as the Emir?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't call him the Emir. Eimen [Realtime transcript read in error "Amin"], Eimen, I think that was the name or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, why did you meet Eimen?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't meet him, I just knew him. I didn't meet him.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if we could have a correction, the name is "Eimen." It's a very important name in this trial, Eimen. That's what the witness said,"Eimen", not "Amin" or whatever. Eimen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you spell it for the benefit of the stenographer, please, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, can you please spell the name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I think the name was, but I really don't know. E-I-M-E-N. Yes, I think it's right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, can you tell us why you met with Eimen?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said a while ago, I didn't meet him. He was simply the only Mujahedin, the only Arab I knew in that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: How did you come to know him, then?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't even remember how we first met. I didn't really meet him in that way. We weren't introduced. I just happened to know his name and who he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But your testimony yesterday says you saw him. "The only person I saw was," as it was recorded yesterday, "the Emir." Now we know it's "Eimen." Where and when did you see him on that occasion, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw him quite often, but I didn't know exactly who he was. I would see him out in the street, in the field, but I didn't know who he was. I never personally met him, in the sense of being introduced to him, but I knew his name and I knew who he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can you elaborate on the answer you just gave to the Judge, Mr. Hajderhodzic, namely, "I would see him out in the street, in the field"? Under what circumstances would you see him in the street and in the field?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, out in the street, like anybody else, you see someone ten times more, you see them, their faces become familiar. It was difficult for me to distinguish between all those people. I saw him several times in certain areas where our units were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And you also went on to say that: "I never personally met him, in the sense of being introduced to him, but I knew his name and I knew who he was." Could you tell us how you knew his name and how you knew who he was?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're talking about his role in the unit, I don't know. I knew he was an Arab. I knew he was a man who was there. I knew he had something to do with the Mujahedin, and that's as much as I knew about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: But, sir, how did you know -- how did you come to know his name?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Someone must have told me. I can't say who. Outsiders knew more about those men than the people from the Division Command like us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. And Eimen, what languages did he speak?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what languages he spoke, but I think his Bosnian was quite bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And how did you know that he spoke Bosnian, sir?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw him communicate with the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And which people are you referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the ordinary people in the field. Well, you can't prohibit somebody from talking to people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Now, if the witness could be shown the document marked for identification 480. I'll note for the record that this document is dated the 13th of September, 1995, and it's addressed to the 35th dKoV command post. If we could now go to page 2 of the B/C/S and page 3 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir -- if we could scroll down on the B/C/S, perhaps. Sir, I'd like to direct your attention to the section marked "4", and it's entitled "Remark," and namely the second bullet point there. And there's a reference there to two companies of the 5th Battalion of the 328th Brigade capturing 61 hostiles. Sir, is this the information -- it's the second bullet point. There are actually two sections marked "4". I apologise for that. It's the section that's marked "Remark," Your Honour. Sir, is this the information on prisoners of war that you had -- that you received during the course of the Farz operation and to which you've referred to during your testimony?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was based on this document that I believe that -- do you want me to clarify this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Yes, if you could, sir.

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. This is the logic behind this reasoning: There was a report from lower-level units which reached the 35th Division. This was for me to receive, to look at, to read, and then based on all these reports, to produce a report that I was to send to the Corps Command. It was actually my responsibility, the responsibility of the Intelligence Department. What date is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If we could go back to the first page.

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to see the date. This is the 13th of September. On the 13th of September -- I don't know, I don't remember my whereabouts on the 13th of September, probably in Hajderovici or somewhere. This was the sort of information that was collected at the command post or the forward command post, and I was at the time at the forward command post, and then it moved from one place to another, and I really don't know why this didn't make the report. The report was put together by men who received information and sent it directly to me. I just signed these things off. Those were the people who were there. Yes, well, I was convinced this would be in my report because it would only be logical for information contained in the combat report of one of the brigades to be included in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, beyond written reports, could you inform us of how you would communicate with your superiors?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were able to communicate perhaps over the phone or face to face, but in the course of combat operations we could communicate on very few occasions or it was, in fact, difficult. Only when the telephone lines were set up it was possible for us to talk over the phone. And during the combat operations, we were so far apart that it was impossible for us to meet face to face at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: You referred to telephone communications, sir. Was this a means that you would use to communicate with your superiors?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what superiors, my superior in the technical terms or with my commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Both, sir.

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was together with the part of the Command of the 35th Division. We moved forward, and only when we set up -- I don't really remember who I talked to, what means of communications we used, but if it was possible to talk over the phone, that's what we did. And as to what I was talking about ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you like to finish your sentence, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say that it is difficult for me to remember any conversations or, in fact, whether there were any conversations at all, because if you go somewhere, if you move forward, and if you change places, if you change command posts, you have to take everything with you, you have to establish the lines, you have to establish communications, you have to set up the whole infrastructure for the communications, and this is very difficult. And often it would happen that we would move to a new command post and we had not established any communications with whoever it was that we were supposed to be in communication with, because the events preempted us. The communications amongst us were carried out either over the phone or face to face. I really don't know in what way. We simply communicated any which way we could. We made due of anything we had at our disposal a thousand and one different ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I was under the impression that Your Honour wanted to put a further question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, I just wanted him to finish his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. I have no further questions for this witness. I would just ask this document be tendered into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 480.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 480. Thank you very much, madam. Any questions, Judge? Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, let us go back for a moment to the prisoners that you saw during your visit in Livade. You told us yesterday that you received, if I understood you correctly, a telephone call, so at any rate you did receive information to the effect that there were prisoners of war there, and now I would like to know who provided you with this information.

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall at this time who it was that gave me this information, or rather I don't remember who gave me the task or, rather, who gave me the information, but that was sufficient for me to go to Zavidovici and to meet the person that I was supposed to go there with. I really don't remember who gave me this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Apart from that, do you remember the wording in the notice that you received? What were you told, specifically, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's different for me to remember the specific words after all this time, because we all strived to forget so many things, but I do remember that it was said that there were prisoners. I don't even remember -- no, I really don't remember. I don't want to speculate now. I don't remember the wording. I just know that I was supposed to meet the assistant commander for security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And were you told there were prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. It may have been said, it may have not been said. I really don't remember what was said and what was not said, because many years have passed, 15 years almost. No, not 15, less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to Operation Farz and what you told us in your cross-examination today, on the basis of a document we were able to find out that there were 400 people who were killed and a large number of injured, some with serious injuries, some with minor injuries. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How did you learn, how did you get to know that there were people with serious or minor injuries, if you did not capture them?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the information that I received from lower-level units, and all this information was then gathered. This is unverified information. This is not something that is used for analysis. It's for the daily reports, and they have yet to be verified, proven and so on. This is the information that was available on that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the wounded, regardless of the seriousness of their injuries, did this include people who were on your side of the front line.

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this report, I did not talk about our units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand that these are the wounded on the enemy's side. Fair enough. But in order to be able to ascertain whether these people had serious or minor injuries, the units that were subordinate to you, or rather units that submitted information to you, should have been able to see those people in order to be able to give you this information; is that not so.

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, whether they actually saw these people or whether this was an assessment based on the number of hits on a target, for the most part those were the assessments for the number of people who were hors de combat. On the basis of -- well, what is important is the assessment. What was important for me was the assessment of the forces on the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hajderhodzic, your testimony has been interesting. It leaves behind some unclarity, and I will try to, in a few questions, to see if I can elicit some more clear information from you. Now, first of all, you told us yesterday that the El Mujahid Detachment was not under the 35th Division's command. If this is so, then, in your view, whose command was the El Mujahid Detachment then under?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very difficult for me to say who commanded the El Mudjahedin Detachment. All I know is that the 35th Division was not happy at all to see those people. These people did not get in frequent with us or they were not in contact with us at all. It is difficult for me to say who it was, but they suddenly showed up there. I don't know. In fact, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say that your division was not happy to see these people there?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we wanted to say that it was not very pleasant if there is somebody else in your area of responsibility and you have no control whatsoever over that somebody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Are you aware of any attempt made by the Command of the 35th Division to acquire control over these, in quotation marks, "somebody"?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what my commander did, but I do know that we were all very unhappy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand that you might be unhappy for the reason that you do not have control over these "somebody," but if they were fighting on your side, any division commander would be appreciative of that assistance, would he not?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe yes and maybe no. Assistance is one thing, and taking over some powers, it's a different thing, because the way these people behaved in the town was as follows: They started mistreating people, shooting at people who were swimming in the river. There was a ban prohibiting young men and women, girls, from holding hands, and so on and so forth, so that normal people felt revulsion when faced with them. And as for this other thing, whether the commander would have been happy or not, this is always a question of how much you're willing to pay for assistance, and the question is whether this was assistance at all. I said then, and this is what I say now, this was no assistance at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did you pay for the assistance or did the 35th Command or anybody else in the ABiH pay for the assistance?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but we are paying the price now, I guess, not in money.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let's move to my second question, which is: The information you gave us that the El Mujahid Detachment was not supposed to take part in the Farz operation in September 1995, do you know if the El Mujahid Detachment actually took part in the Farz operation?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. And do you know why I don't know? I don't know that because the time has taught me that I can only believe the things that I see with my own eyes. Some things that I was sure were one way turned out to be completely the opposite. I didn't see the disposition of these people. I didn't see the place where they started from, and I didn't see where they were moving, so I was very mistrustful then, as far as they were concerned, and I remain mistrustful to this date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hajderhodzic, you were also the assistant commander of Intelligence, so you were not supposed to run around in the field and see for yourself what was going on. There was a system in place that would provide you with ample information about what was going on during combat. And I find it hard to believe, to be honest, that you did not receive, from the people involved in this system of information, that you did not receive information about the activities of the El Mujahid Detachment, whether you trusted these people or not.

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Previously, I said that I was only interested in things that were on the other side of the front line. They were on this side of the front line, and let me tell you something now. This was really not within my purview, but I tried to understand their organisation, who they were and so on, and in spite of all the efforts made in good faith, I was unable to achieve any spectacular results, I was unable to learn anything. I really didn't come to grasp their organisation. The only thing that I did learn was that they had people who would mingle with other people and people who were in some other place and that they would seen by very few. So that I wanted to divide this into two segments, the secular part, so to speak, that had its own goals, and the combat element, and that is why I didn't -- they were a very tight community, difficult to penetrate, and they were particularly mistrustful of me because my assistant was a Croat, an ethnic Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: My question to you was if you knew that the El Mujahid Detachment had taken part in the Farz operation, and I'm a bit unsure about the answer to that question. Did you or did you not know that they had taken part?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew, on the basis of combat documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like to move on to my third question, which relates to your knowledge about the prisoners of war who had been detained by the El Mujahid Detachment. We have had evidence in this case that suggests that in August, in late August, 1995, a group of 11 prisoners of war were transferred from the El Mujahid camp in Kamenica to the KP Dom in Zenica, that is to say, to the authorities of the ABiH. And again, Mr. Hajderhodzic, I find it difficult to believe that you would not in some way be involved in the arrangements for that transfer. As the assistant commander of Intelligence of the 35th Division, I assume that you were involved in one way or another, or at least that you heard about this transfer that took place in late August 1995. Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, believe it or not, I did not take part in it and I didn't know when these people were transferred to the 3rd Corps, because this was not in the purview of the intelligence organ. The other people were in charge of that, and of that I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And did you hear about the transfer?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, war is a whole different ball game. You can hear all kinds of things. There's all kinds of information flying around. It is difficult to select what is true and what is not true. I don't remember all those stories that I heard in that period. To tell you the truth, I simply can't concentrate and actually sift, from all this information, what is true and what is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: My question was not about whether it was truthful or not. My question was if you actually heard about the transfer.

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I may have heard from someone, rather, but officially no one told me and I wasn't aware of the transfer. I don't even believe that I heard at all, on second thought. I don't remember. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I accept your answer, although I still find it difficult to believe that the transfer of 11 enemy prisoners would not have caught your interest. These people might be in possession of valuable information, and I'm sure that you, as assistant commander of Intelligence, would have wanted to elicit information from these gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, given the fact that we did not often have an opportunity to speak to POWs, or I didn't, because there were none, virtually, we didn't have a detention unit, or a prison, or anything that would have pointed me in that direction, that would have given me the option of talking to someone 15 or 20 days later -- you refer to a date. I forget the date. I always try to link this up with something else. I was certain that if anyone went to the corps, all the information would be recorded by someone from our superior command. Quite simply, I wasn't aware of that. Even if I had known, I probably would have done something -- perhaps I would have done something, but the truth of the matter is I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hajderhodzic, it is time for us to take a break now, but before we do so, I'd like to put a question to you, and then you can have the break to think about the answer. I also wish to remind you again, as the Presiding Judge has done, that you took a declaration yesterday and today that you would speak the truth, and the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. And I think it is important for you to seek to establish the truth at this trial. Let's have a break and let's meet at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hajderhodzic, I realised only when I came out of the courtroom that I forgot to put the question to you that I wanted before the break. I apologise for that, but I don't expect your answer to be any different. The question that I have is this: Were you at any time instructed, ordered, or suggested not to include information on the El Mujahid Detachment or activities of other Mujahedin groups in your reports?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was never instructed to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Hajderhodzic, I thought I heard you say, and I would like to confirm with you, that you didn't know that the El Mudjahedin Detachment had been subordinated to the 35th Division. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In fact, you didn't know that the El Mudjahedin Detachment had been a unit of the ARBiH?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that, either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In fact, you also did not know the establishment of the El Mudjahedin Detachment, you didn't know how large they were?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, all these questions are connected, and my answers are much the same. As for the El Mudjahedin Detachment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just say "yes," "no," or, "I don't know." I'm asking you these questions because I'm a bit puzzled by some of the answers you gave today, and here's what puzzles me: How do you know that the group belonging to Abu Zubeir Al Halili was not part of Mujahedin, a Mujahedin detachment?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, I heard of such units that were around the area, but I never saw a written document or anything like that to base this belief on. It is something that people were saying and something I heard, that there was some units there or something. Believe me, I don't even know that the El Mujahedin unit was established, or under whose command, or where it was. I never saw them all lined up for review. I never saw the unit in its entirety. I never had a chance to judge the structure of its command or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Hajderhodzic, I'm going to ask you once more to please listen to the question and answer the question, and the question only. I'm asking you a very simple question, and don't repeat things that you've already told me. My question to you was: How do you know that the group belonging to Abu Zubeir Al Halili was not part of the Mujahedin, the El Mudjahedin Detachment? You don't know anything about the El Mudjahedin Detachment, you don't know who are the members of the El Mudjahedin Detachment. I want to know how you come to the conclusion that the group belonging to Abu Zubeir has nothing to do with El Mudjahedin Detachment.

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say for sure, but in certain constellations there is talk of the El Mudjahedin Detachment, and in certain other constellations there is talk of these other guys. These are two totally separate groups, or at least that's how the story went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So when you said it as a fact this afternoon or this morning, you were really not telling something that you knew for a fact?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, in situations like these, facts, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you also don't know whether the Hamdala was part of the El Mudjahedin Detachment, do you know?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, I assume not, but, no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: See, let me warn you once again. We would like to extract from you facts, not assumptions. When you assume, at least do say that's your assumption. Then we know how to handle that.

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, let me turn to the topic of the prisoners of war. You also said this morning that you wrote a report to the 3rd Corps about prisoners of war. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you were shown a whole lot of reports that were written, signed by you, in which the prisoners of war were not mentioned. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, you have now been shown Exhibit 480, which was -- can we put Exhibit 480 on the screen, please. Do you see that report?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now this -- earlier today, when you were being examined by the Prosecutor, he asked you the question -- this question starts at line 25 of page 54: "Sir, is this the information on prisoners of war that you had, that you received during the course of the Farz operation, and to which you have referred to during your testimony?" And your answer was: "Yes, it was based on this document that I believe that --" And then: "Do you want me to clarify this?" What I want to confirm with you is, when you say, "Yes, it was based on this document," do you now remember this document? Have you seen this document before today?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the day? Yes, I remember. Yes, I remember that I saw it before today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where did you see it and when was that?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I no longer know where I saw this or that, but I do believe that I saw this report in Sarajevo as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me ask you this question, then: When you said to the Defence counsel that you had written a report to the 3rd Corps about prisoners of war, was that report based on this document?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, you're asking me to answer "yes" or "no" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And there's a third alternative. If you don't know, then you say you don't know, and then we don't go further, we don't waste time on it. You either say "yes" or "no" or, "I don't know," or, "I can't remember."

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember and I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And if you can't remember, then that's the end of my questions. I can't take my questions any further. Thank you very much. Any questions arising from the questions from the Bench? Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Well, there's one question, and there may be a follow-up question to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, in response to a question that His Honour Judge Harhoff had put to you, you answered,"The only thing that I" -- and this is in relation to the El Mudjahedin Detachment, and it appears, actually, the witness's answer begins at -- the relevant portion of the witness's answer begins at page 62, line 21 of the transcript from today. And this is the relevant portion of your answer, Mr. Hajderhodzic, and it relates to the El Mudjahedin Detachment: "The only thing that I did learn was that they had people who would mingle with other people." Now, which people from the El Mudjahedin Detachment are you referring to when you say "They had people who would mingle with other people"?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you a single name, but those were people I could see in the street and around the area, those who came into contact with civilians and soldiers in the Zavidovici area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Menon. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I do have a question. Further cross-examination by Ms. Vidovic:

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Witness, His Honour, Harhoff, asked you about the Mujahedin, and on page 61, lines 34 and 35, you describe their behaviour, so I want you to clarify something for the benefit of the record. You said they started mistreating people, and then the record reflected "They fired at people who were swimming." What I understood you to be saying is fired shots above the heads of those swimming in the river.

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they fired shots into the air to scare those people off, to not take off their clothes and not get out of the river without their clothes on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: It is true, isn't it, that the incidents that they were causing and that you heard about, and I mean the Mujahedin, had to do with their different views on religion and life, different from those held by the local Muslims; would I be right in stating that?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: You never heard that those people were indeed killing anyone at all, POWs included, before you were in touch with them in July?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: You didn't know anything like that?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: You didn't know that they were mistreating POWs?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I knew nothing about that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now go back to one of the last questions asked by His Honour, the Presiding Judge Moloto. You were asked about a group of these Mujahedin. The Judge asked you this: "How do you know that Abu Zubeir and the Hamdala were not part of the El Mudjahedin Detachment?" And I'm asking you this: Based on your evidence, the evidence that you gave today about not knowing anything about the El Mujahid, how on earth could you possibly know this at all? Do you see my suggestion? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: How could you have known otherwise that they were members of the El Mudjahedin Detachment, for example?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. What I do know is that different names were used and that's all I can base my judgement on, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Please, Witness, please, is it true that among the people of Zavidovici, in the area there were stories, rumours, circulating at the time about various groups of Arabs?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Those Arabs in the area were not a single body, they weren't unified; there were several different scattered groups, separate groups; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the rumours were about. Those are stories. I have no documents to show for this and so that is why I expressed the reservations that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: So you heard the stories?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: You will agree that today during your testimony and yesterday on several occasions, you did say you heard stories; right?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Stories, stories, rumours, not just about this being a story or a rumour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Slow down, slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: While testifying yesterday and today, you mentioned stories. This is not the only story that you testified to; right?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, that brings us to the end of your testimony. Thank you very much for coming to testify. You are now excused. You may stand down. Travel well back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could the Chamber move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Will you please make the declaration then, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: For the record, sir, can you please state your full name, and spell both your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: Sejfulah Mrkaljevic, S-E-J-F-U-L-A-H, M-R-K-A-L-J-E-V-I-C.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, for the record, can you please provide your date of birth and place of birth?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 2nd of September, 1959, in Kotorsko, the municipality of Doboj, Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkaljevic, can you tell the Trial Chamber how you were employed, where you were employed, at the time the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina commenced?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: Up until the time when the war started in Bosnia and Herzegovina in April 1992, I had a job in the coal mine in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you remain in that job at the coal mine, sir, once the war began in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: When the war started in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I left my job in the Zenica coal mine and I volunteered to join the regular units of the BH Army because I wanted to take part in defending Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkaljevic, could you please briefly tell the Trial Chamber what units of the BH Army you were assigned to from the time you joined the BH Army until you left the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, that's in April 1992, I reported to the Zenica Municipal Staff, the Defence Staff in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what, sir, were your duties at the Zenica Municipal Staff, and how long did you remain in that position?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: In the Municipal Defence Staff in Zenica, I was appointed the deputy commander of the Counter-Sabotage Platoon, and I was at that post until mid-May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what post, if any, did you assume in mid-May 1992?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: In accordance with the orders of my superiors in the Municipal Defence Staff in Zenica, I was transferred to the 1st Zenica Brigade of the Territorial Defence, or rather the 1st Zenica Brigade of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was the deputy battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, which battalion of the 1st Zenica Brigade were you the deputy battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: When I came to the 1st Zenica Brigade of the BH Army, I was the deputy commander -- I was appointed the deputy commander of the 1st Battalion of the 1st Zenica Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how long, sir, did you remain in that position as the deputy commander of the 1st Battalion of the 1st Zenica Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: I was the deputy commander of the 1st Battalion of the 1st Zenica Brigade of the BH Army for a short period of time, until sometime in early June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, in early June 1992, which unit, if any, did you join?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: I was the commander of the 1st Battalion of the 1st Zenica Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how long did you remain in that position, sir?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: I was the commander of the 1st Battalion of the 1st Zenica Brigade until I was seriously wounded, which was on the 14th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Following this serious wounding that you received, did you rejoin any unit of the BH Army, and if so, which unit?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: After I was wounded, I received treatment until the end of February, early March, 1993, and then despite the fact that I was not completely well, I returned to the Command of the 1st Zenica Brigade, or rather while I was away, the brigade was transformed in accordance with the restructuring of the BH Army, and it became the 303rd Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And for purposes of clarification, sir, did you rejoin or did you join the 303rd Mountain Brigade upon your return from medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I rejoined them. As I said, I was not completely well, but I came back in order to help my colleagues, my fellow fighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, when you rejoined the 303rd Mountain Brigade, what were your responsibilities and duties?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: Upon my arrival in the Command of the 303rd Mountain Brigade, the brigade commander, Mr. Suad Hasanovic assigned me in view of my condition in the operation and training organ of the Brigade Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how long, Mr. Mrkaljevic, did you remain with the 303rd Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: I was in the operations and training organ of the 303rd Mountain Brigade until mid-May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, what unit, if any, did you join in mid-May 1993?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: In accordance with the instructions and the orders of my superiors, in the first half of May 1993 I was transferred to the Command of the 3rd Corps of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what were your responsibilities upon being assigned to the 3rd Corps of the BH Army in mid-May 1993?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: In mid-May 1993, I was appointed to the intelligence organ of the 3rd Corps Command. At first, my duties involved intelligence processing. That period lasted a month and a half. And after that, I did the analytical processing of intelligence that was coming in, into the intelligence organ or, rather, the Intelligence Department of the 3rd Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkaljevic, after joining the intelligence organ of the 3rd Corps in mid-May 1993, how long did you remain with the 3rd Corps intelligence organ?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: I was in the intelligence organ of the 3rd Corps until the 3rd Corps was disbanded, but there was a short break, a month and a half. That was the period while I was appointed to the Command of the 319th Mountain Brigade in Zepce. So that was in November and until mid-December 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just so we're clear, sir, other than this break from November until mid-December 1993, when you were with the 319th Mountain Brigade, other than that time period, sir, you were with the 3rd Corps intelligence organ from mid-May 1993 until the end of the war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Except for that period, I spent the entire war until the 3rd Corps was disbanded. I was the head of the analysis section in the Intelligence Department of the 3rd Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention, sir, to the issue of ranks in the ABiH. When you first joined the 3rd Corps, sir, did you hold any type of military rank?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: When I joined the 3rd Corps, or in fact at the moment when I joined the ranks of the regular Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the former Yugoslav People's Army, in 1977 -- no, I apologise. That was in 1978, and 1979 I graduated from the reserve officers school that was in Zadar. I was in air defence, rocket and artillery units branch. When I left the Yugoslav People's Army, the former Yugoslav People's Army, I was given the rank of a reserve second lieutenant. I was a junior officer in the former Yugoslav People's Army. And after that -- and all the way up to the period when the aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina started in 1992, I was promoted to the rank of a reserve lieutenant in the former Yugoslav People's Army. In accordance with the procedures stipulated by law that defined the reserve force of the former Yugoslav People's Army in the former Socialist Federated Republic of Yugoslavia, I could not have been given a higher rank because I did not have enough exercises to my name. I didn't participate in a sufficient number of exercises in my branch of service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. When you joined the BH Army, did that army have any ranks?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: No. At first, there were no ranks. There were just posts and duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time, sir, when ranks were introduced?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: Ranks were introduced, and the first conference of ranks was carried out in August 1994. In fact, that is when I received a rank, myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, what rank did you receive in August 1994?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: I was promoted to the rank of a captain of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness now be shown the document marked P01771. P01771. And we'll start by taking a look at the first page of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkaljevic, do you see the document on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what this document is?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: This is a document originating from the Supreme Command Staff of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, listing people who were promoted to certain ranks, or rather this is a proposal on the part of the Supreme Command of the BH Armed Forces sent to the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina for the people whose names are listed below to be promoted to certain ranks in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask, with the assistance of the Registrar, that we go to page 3 in Bosnian and page 8 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you see where it says: "D, Rank of Captain"?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Item D, yes. Item D in this document, I can see my name on this list and also the duty I had in the 3rd Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just so we're all clear, Mr. Mrkaljevic, can you tell us where, in relation to the subheading "D, Rank of Captain," your name appears?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: My name is the first name on this list under item D.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I would ask this document be admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit number 570.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness now be shown the document previously marked as P01779. P01779. And, again, we'll start with the first page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkaljevic, do you see the document on the screen in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us what this document is, please?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: This is a decision of the Presidency, listing the people who were promoted, as of the date of this decision, to the ranks as per the proposal submitted by the General Staff of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can we please now, with the assistance of the Registrar, please go to page 6 in the Bosnian version and page 10 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I draw your attention, sir, to the subheading "D" to the rank of captain.

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: Under item D, the "Rank of Captain," the fifth entry contains my full name and my duty in the 3rd Corps Command. That's on this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. The Prosecution would ask this document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit number 571.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you see the date on this document?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: The date on this document is the 5th of August, 1994, and we also have the reference number listed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mrkaljevic, I'd like to turn your attention to the midsummer of 1995, that is, the period in June/July 1995. What position within the 3rd Corps intelligence organ were you holding at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, I was the chief of the analysis section in the Intelligence Department of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber, sir, how many people were in the intelligence organ of the 3rd Corps at that point in time, that is, the summer of 1995?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: In the summer of 1995, there were somewhere between 12 and 14 personnel on various jobs in the Intelligence Department in the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, who was in charge of the Intelligence Department in the 3rd Corps at that time, summer 1995?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: At that time in 1995, the assistant commander for Intelligence in the 3rd Corps Command was Mr. Edin Husic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us, Mr. Mrkaljevic, that you were the head of the analysis section. How many people, in the summer of 1995, were in the 3rd Corps Intelligence Department analysis section?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: In the summer of 1995, the analysis section of the Intelligence Department of the 3rd Corps contained two officers, apart from myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How was the Intelligence Department of the 3rd Corps structured in the summer of 1995?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: In the summer of 1995, the 3rd Corps Intelligence Department had its subsections, the subsection for analysis and intelligence processing, intelligence planning of reconnaissance activities, the section for relations and cooperation with the representatives of foreign armies and international organisations in the 3rd Corps area, a section for electronic reconnaissance and surveillance, so that these four sections covered the entire range of activities of the 3rd Corps Command Intelligence Department, and the section for electronic reconnaissance and surveillance had another subsection. It was called "Special Operations."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please explain or briefly explain the section for relations and cooperation with the representatives of foreign armies and international organisations? Can you tell us what that -- what that's all about?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: It was a service. Three people worked there. And all the representatives of the foreign armies and international organisations who were present in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps were not supposed to go directly to the 3rd Corps Command, lest they should waste time. They contacted this section.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you perhaps explain who these foreign armies were and what they were doing in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: The term "foreign armies" referred to the SFOR troops, the multinational SFOR troops, and in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps, this referred to all those elements of SFOR present there, all the issues that they wanted to raise, everything that they needed. They talked to the section for relations with foreign armies and international organisations, and at the same time this section acted as a liaison office with the Command of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkaljevic, other than your assignment as head of the analysis section of the 3rd Corps Intelligence Department, did you have any other duties or responsibilities during the summer of 1995?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to my duties as the chief of the analysis section, I was the deputy assistant commander for Intelligence in the 3rd Corps Command in the absence of Mr. Edin Husic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell the Trial Chamber, sir, how the Intelligence Department of the 3rd Corps functioned, in terms of reporting requirements? To whom did Mr. Husic or, in his absence, you, as his deputy assistant commander, report?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: In the Intelligence Department of the 3rd Corps Command, there were two chains of command. In technical and professional terms, there was the vertical reporting line to the Intelligence Administration of the Joint Command of the Armed Forces or the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and horizontally the reporting line went to the commander of the 3rd Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us, Mr. Mrkaljevic, if you know, when you say "vertical reporting line to the Intelligence Administration of the Joint Command of the Armed Forces or the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina," to whom was the 3rd Corps sending its reports, the 3rd Corps Intelligence Department sending its reports?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: The reports that were drafted in the Intelligence Department of the 3rd Corps Command were sent to the Intelligence Administration of the BH Army General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And where was that Intelligence Administration of the BH Army General Staff located?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: The Intelligence Administration of the BH Army General Staff was in Sarajevo, and in Kakanj, in a hotel there. There was always a certain number of officers from the Intelligence Administration who were there in order to be able to provide assistance, some kind of a rapid intervention unit to assist any of the intelligence organs in the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And would the reports from the intelligence organ or Intelligence Department of the 3rd Corps go to Sarajevo, or Kakanj, or both?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: They went mostly to Sarajevo, and when needed -- or rather when the superior officer issued an order to that effect, they went to Kakanj too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, if you know, who was the head of the Intelligence Administration of the BH Army General Staff?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: The chief of the Intelligence Administration in the BH Army General Staff was the late Mr. Mustafa Hajrulahovic Talijan. He was a general of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And where was General Mustafa Hajrulahovic Talijan located?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: His headquarters were in Sarajevo. I think that this was the building of the Sarajevo Novi Grad District Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And do you know, sir, which members of the BH Army General Staff Intelligence Administration were located in Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you the exact names of the people who were in Kakanj, but most -- for the most part, those would be officers from the Intelligence Administration, and they were rotated in shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mrkaljevic, can you tell us a little bit about how the 3rd Corps Intelligence Department received information or reports from subordinate or lower-level 3rd Corps units?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: From the lower-level units in the 3rd Corps, the reports came in in accordance with the developments in the field, from the assistant commanders for Intelligence at the level of divisions, and assistant commanders for Intelligence at brigade level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkaljevic, when you say "assistant commanders for Intelligence at the level of divisions," which divisions are we talking about or are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: In the summer of 1995, the 3rd Corps Command had as its element the 35th Division in Zavidovici and the 37th Division in Tesanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, who were the assistant commanders for Intelligence in those two divisions?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: In this time period, the assistant commander in the 35th Division was Mr. Izudin Hajderhodzic, and in the 37th Division in Tesanj, I can't recall the name, but I do know that for a brief period of time in 1995, the commander for Intelligence in the 37th Division, there were three people who actually were appointed to that post over a very brief period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, you also told us, as reflected on lines 3 and 4 of page 88, that you received reports from assistant commanders for Intelligence at brigade level. Can you tell us which brigades were supplying reports to the 3rd Corps Intelligence Department?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: The 7th Muslim Brigade, the 314th, the 313th and the 303rd Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, these four brigades that you've just mentioned, the 7th, 314th, 330th and 303rd, why did they report directly to the 3rd Corps Intelligence Department?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it 330th or 313th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 330 Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: They reported directly to the Command, the Command of the Intelligence Department of the 3rd Corps whenever they were not resubordinated to one of the divisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you briefly explain, Mr. Mrkaljevic, what the function of the analysis section of the Intelligence Department of the 3rd Corps was?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: Within the Intelligence Department of the 3rd Corps Command, the analysis section was the section that analytically processed all incoming information, all intelligence-related incoming information. It would also classify this information and cross-reference it to any other incoming information relating to other issues, information from our neighbours. In keeping with that, the section produced reports, intelligence assessments, and drew conclusions as to the intelligence situation that prevailed in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you give us, sir, some examples of the types of information that was incoming which your section analysed?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: The intelligence section of the 3rd Corps Command was receiving intelligence-related information from any available sources and from our neighbours. When I say "available sources," the work and the function itself of the intelligence section was based on the proper working and functioning of the intelligence services belonging to armies throughout the world. I must say, though, that at the time we didn't have the means or the possibilities normally at the disposal of most other armies. Nevertheless, the focus of our work was this: There was information streaming in from observation posts, where observers were observing the front end, where the clashes were occurring with the enemy. The media were being monitored, too. One studied any document seized from the enemy. The relevant literature was studied, whatever available. The media were studied, and I mean the press. Whenever any printed media could be obtained, information would be processed that was obtained from the prisoners, if any. Information was processed received from displaced persons, people who were driven out of areas now controlled by the Army of Republika Srpska and the HVO, and this was at a time when clashes were ongoing between us and them. Information was processed that we obtained by using radio surveillance and communications surveillance, electronic communication surveillance. All of this information was pooled into the analysis sector. Whatever this incoming information happened to be, urgent, high priority or not, or if it could be dealt with over the near term, perhaps, the chief of the Intelligence Department would always be the first to be informed. He was supposed to monitor the intelligence situation and be familiar with it at any point in time as it pertained to the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. Once all of this information was in, this would trigger a number of different activities within the analysis sector, in order to achieve intelligence data that would be timely, accurate and comprehensive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who were your neighbours from whom you also received intelligence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our neighbours at the time who made their intelligence available to us were the Commands of the 2nd and 7th Corps of the BH Army; rather, whenever necessary, this was also the Command of the 1st Corps of the BH Army, and whenever the need arose, the intelligence command of the 5th Corps of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly, Mr. Mrkaljevic, the role of the Intelligence Department as it relates to the work of military planning and military operations?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC
utterances.text: In the analysis sector, there is the department for operative activities. It would plan activities for the reconnaissance unit attached to the 3rd Corps Command, the 3rd Reconnaissance and Sabotage Company, in keeping with the needs and requirements dictated by the situation on the ground and in compliance with any orders from the 3rd Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mrkaljevic. I believe this would be the appropriate time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is, indeed. Thank you very much. Sir, we can't finish with your evidence. We've come to the end of the day today. We'll come back tomorrow at 9.00 in the same court. Okay? Court adjourned until 9.00 in Courtroom II.
